# A fast-forward merge - what `git pull` usually is - runs no finalize and no
# post-checkout, so nothing used to refresh the revealed plaintext. The next seal
# then wrote our stale version back over what we just pulled. post-merge reveals
# the objects the merge brought in.

exec git init
exec git config user.email test@sesam.dev
exec git config user.name 'Sesam Test'

cp base.txt $TMPDIR/base.txt
cp changed.txt $TMPDIR/changed.txt

exec sesam init --user admin --install-merge
exec git add -A
exec git commit -m 'init sesam'

cp $TMPDIR/base.txt s
exec sesam add s --group admin
exec git add -A
exec git commit -m 'add secret'

exec git checkout -b topic
cp $TMPDIR/changed.txt s
exec sesam seal
exec git add -A
exec git commit -m 'topic: change s'

# Nothing on our side, so this fast-forwards.
exec git checkout master
exec git merge topic
stdout 'Fast-forward'

# The revealed file followed the object instead of staying behind.
exec cat s
stdout 'CHANGED'
exec sesam status
! stdout 'out of sync'

# And sealing keeps it, rather than reverting to BASE.
exec sesam seal
exec sesam show .sesam/objects/s.sesam
stdout 'CHANGED'
exec sesam verify
stderr 'Integrity: ok'

-- base.txt --
line one
BASE
line three
-- changed.txt --
line one
CHANGED
line three
